item.title: ‘Go Get Your Kicks’: The Europeans Obsessed With a U.S. Highway
item.description:
Wolfgang Werz took a drag on his cigarette and a sip from his coffee cup, looked at his watch and blew his whistle. It was 8 a.m. in the parking lot of the Best Western in suburban St. Louis, time for Mr. Werz to rally his troops — a dozen German and Swiss tourists — so they could jump on their Harley Davidson motorcycles and head out on Route 66.

Mr. Werz, who is 67, rattled off the day’s stops on their roughly 200-mile stretch through Missouri: the Wagon Wheel Motel in Cuba; the rocking chair in Fanning; the Devil’s Elbow Bridge; the Redmon’s Candy shop in Phillipsburg; and, by about 5 p.m., Springfield, the birthplace of the highway known as the “The Main Street of America.”

Then Mr. Werz, a wiry, weather-beaten former ski instructor from Tubingen, Germany, looked at the group of middle-aged bikers in leather jackets and boots and gave them their marching orders on day three of their two-week, 2,500-mile sojourn from Chicago to Santa Monica, Calif.: “Let’s go get your kicks.”

The “Mother Road,” as John Steinbeck dubbed Route 66 in “The Grapes of Wrath,” turns 100 this year, and the motels, diners and gas stations along the road have repaired their neon signs, refreshed their menus and stocked their shelves with commemorative goods for the flood of extra traffic. Tourism boards and Route 66 associations have held classic car rallies, street painting contests and art installations, including a 23-foot stained-glass-style push pin that marks the midpoint of the road in Oklahoma.

No one buys a ticket to visit Route 66, so numbers on how many tourists it attracts are imprecise. A Rutgers University study in 2011 estimated about $132 million in annual spending along the highway. Jennifer Wilding, a community engagement adviser at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, whose domain includes four states intersected by Route 66, expects spending to be markedly higher during the centennial. The amount is probably less than a week’s worth of revenue at Disney World, but it is meaningful to small businesses.

The shops along Route 66 lean into their location, and as I drove sections of the route with Mr. Werz and his group this year, business owners said the anniversary was providing a significant financial boost.

International tourists are among the biggest sources of spending. More than one-third of visitors, by some counts, are from overseas. There are Route 66 associations throughout Europe and South America, as well as in Japan, Australia and beyond. Shopkeepers say that international travelers stay longer and spend more than Americans, who are typically older and buy less.

Jennifer Brennan, the co-owner of the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Mo., said sales had jumped about 50 percent this summer, with magnets, bracelets, and salt and pepper shakers selling especially well. “We’ve been ordering like crazy to keep up,” she said, adding that 120 international motorcyclists had stopped by that day.

Roberto Vannelli, the most gung-ho member of Mr. Werz’s group, bought 16 T-shirts by the time he made it to Arizona. Peter Fordemann and his wife, Katja Weinert, spent about $10,000 each to join Mr. Werz’s tour, a bucket list item that included flights from Germany and motorcycles they rented in Des Plaines, Ill.

Patrick Tuttle, the director of Visit Joplin, in Missouri, said visitors from 45 countries signed the guest book in city hall last year, when people from outside the United States spent $5.7 million in Joplin — the majority of whom were probably travelers on Route 66.

Mike Cowen, who turned a gas station into a gift shop in Williams, Ariz., said about 60 percent of his customers were from abroad.

Yet it can be an edgy time for international visitors to travel through America.

Sam Murray, who guides New Zealanders on Route 66, said some customers canceled their reservations this summer because they were nervous about the political climate. The strong U.S. dollar, combined with higher gas prices, airfares and travel insurance, also played a role.

But largely, Route 66 felt like an apolitical haven. International visitors told me they were reluctant to wade into political debates they had little stake in. Shopkeepers and restaurant owners did not want to alienate their customers by airing their own views.

“Friends say to me, ‘You can’t go to the U.S. now,’” Mr. Werz said. “I always say, every country has its problems. Presidents come and go. Route 66 stays the same.”

For decades, Route 66 was the quickest way to drive across the country for sharecroppers escaping the Dust Bowl, soldiers reporting for duty and travelers relocating. That last group included my parents, who moved from Brooklyn to Los Angeles in 1960. The road was filled with motels advertising air conditioning and color television, stores hawking souvenirs and restaurants that would soon be mythologized in the movie “American Graffiti.”

But as the interstate highway system expanded, many towns along Route 66 were bypassed and withered. The last stretch was bypassed in Williams, Ariz., when I-40 opened a few miles away, and the entire road was federally decommissioned in 1985.

Not long after, Angel Delgadillo, a barber in Seligman, Ariz., helped form the Historic Route 66 Association, which convinced the state to erect “Historic Route 66” signs to draw tourists back to their towns. The other seven states along the road followed.

It worked. Thousands of tourists trying to relive the era of road maps, station wagons and full-service filling stations returned to Route 66, even though it was no longer a contiguous artery. Route 66 enthusiasts speak reverently about the road, like Trekkies or model train nerds. The Route 66 Sentinel, a magazine whose slogan is “Watchdog of the Mother Road,” never seems to run out of material. Some “roadies” collect pins, shot glasses and other tchotchkes.

Some international fans said they learned about the road from Steinbeck’s book or the namesake Bobby Troup song. Raised in Germany, Mr. Werz said he fell in love with Westerns, classic cars and images of the American West.

“I grew up watching ‘Lassie,’ ‘Bonanza’ and John Wayne movies, and this was always America to me — the diners, neon signs, cars, and cowboys and Indians,” said Mr. Werz, who has Route 66 tattoos on both arms.

On his first trip on the route in 2009, Mr. Werz was struck by the friendliness of Americans. He returned the next year and the year after, when he brought his friend Anja. She loved the trip so much that after they finished in California, they went to Las Vegas and got married.

Wolfgang and Anja started a nonprofit group and have led about 20 tours, becoming minor celebrities. When their group visited Gary’s Gay Parita, a roadside museum in Ash Grove, Mo., the owners, Barb Turner Barnes and her husband, George, hugged Wolfgang and Anja like old friends.

Ms. Barnes said she loved international visitors. Plenty of Americans stop by, of course, but they are often in a rush. “We as a culture aren’t built for the contemplative,” she said. The walls of her gift shop were covered with stickers left by tourists from Costa Rica, Japan and elsewhere.

Roberto Rossi, who runs a Route 66 Association in Italy and wrote “Route 66: An American Myth,” agreed. The vistas are gorgeous and the sense of freedom palpable, but befriending people along the road is the main reason he has returned many times since his first trip in 1990.

“To me, Route 66 is not simply a road,” he wrote in an email. “It is a family that begins in Chicago and ends at the Santa Monica Pier.”

Several shopkeepers told me that international travelers wanted to see the “real America.” A better description might have been a “lost America,” when Route 66 was in its heyday before interstate highways plowed through the country.

As I traveled parts of the route, I was reminded, though, that the heyday was not universal, especially along stretches of the road where Jim Crow laws were enforced and people of color were unwelcome in many establishments.

Outside Oklahoma City, the Threatt Filling Station, one of the few Black-owned gas stations on Route 66, was a poignant reminder of that period. The station was an oasis for Black travelers in search of gas, food and a campground to avoid so-called sundown towns, which excluded people of color after dark into the 1960s.

“If you were a white traveler, your experience on the road would be a lot different than a Black traveler,” said Trait Thompson, the executive director of the Oklahoma History Society. “We tend to look back on the past with rose-colored glasses and with nostalgia, but it wasn’t that way for everyone.”

As Route 66 enters its second century, people along the road wonder what the future holds. During the road’s first renaissance in the 1990s, the journey appealed mainly to older Americans who had traveled Route 66 decades earlier. Then came the baby boomers, whose parents drove the road.

Michael Wallis, who in 1990 published “Route 66: The Mother Road,” is credited with igniting a renewed interest in the road. He was also the voice of the Sheriff in the 2006 Pixar film “Cars,” which takes place in a fictional Route 66 town, Radiator Springs. The movie has introduced younger fans to the road. Replica cars from the movie sit outside gas stations to attract families.

In Seligman, busloads of tourists speaking Mandarin and Spanish continue to stop at Angel Delgadillo’s old barbershop gift shop. Currencies from 166 countries are stapled to the ceiling.

Social media has helped shops and restaurants reach new fans. The Big Texan Steak Ranch in Amarillo, Texas, livestreams customers who try to win a free 72-ounce steak, plus a potato, salad and shrimp cocktail if they finish it all in one hour. Dozens of videos of the contests circulate widely on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. When Mr. Werz’s group arrived, Mariano Moesges, a burly woodworker from Hannover, Germany, tried and failed to finish the meal.

“We’re a wet canvas, and people are painting it,” said Bobby Lee, the restaurant’s owner.

The entire road is a kind of canvas. Many towns feature murals painted on building walls and vintage neon signs on storefronts. Musical roads, with bumps on the street that play a song when you ride over them, were built in Tulsa, Okla., where drivers can hear Woody Guthrie’s anthem “This Land Is Your Land.”

“Until you’re on it, you don’t see it,” said Rhys Martin, director of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association and manager of Preserve Route 66 for the National Trust for Historic Preservation, and whose wife, Samantha Extance, worked on the musical road. “You can put your stamp on it.”

Only toward the end of their trip did Mr. Werz’s group begin to reflect on all they had seen. Taking two weeks to drive 2,500 miles might seem like a lot of time, but the group was busy, making half a dozen or more stops a day. They drove through New Mexico, made a detour into southern Utah (posing for a photo where Tom Hanks stopped running in the movie “Forrest Gump”), took helicopter rides over the Grand Canyon and traversed the Arizona Sidewinder, an eight-mile stretch with 191 hairpin turns at steep elevations with few guardrails. Each evening, they pulled into a motel parking lot, grabbed their bags from the S.U.V. that Anja drove, opened cold cans of Budweiser and relived the day.

The official end of Route 66 is at the intersection of Lincoln and Olympic Boulevards in Santa Monica, where it connects to the Pacific Coast Highway.

But for the German and Swiss bikers, and for many other travelers, their trip concluded not at the route’s actual finish line, but on a pier about a mile away.

That’s where Ian Bowen hawks souvenirs out of a hut next to a sign that reads “End of the Trail.” Mr. Bowen is a Route 66 geek, but he is also an interpretive vessel for the thousands of pilgrims who finish their journey exhausted yet exuberant at his little shop.

Every year, Mr. Bowen sells a couple thousand commemorative certificates for $10 each to customers who clutch them proudly. The certificates are hokey, but they help keep the memory of the journey alive.

“I know that when people are on the trip, they’re sharing pictures with friends and family and posting some stuff on social media, but I want them getting asked about it 10 years later,” Mr. Bowen said.

In mid-June, Mr. Werz’s tour arrived at Mr. Bowen’s shack and almost everyone bought a certificate. (Mr. Werz also provides his own in German.) The trip had been exhilarating, and for many of the participants, the everyday Americans they met stood out. As Jim Hinckley, a historian of the road and friend of Wolfgang and Anja, said during a stop in Kingman, Ariz.: “Route 66 — it’s the people. It’s a highway that doesn’t even exist.”

Having made the journey dozens of times, Wolfgang and Anja told their group knowingly that they would not fully grasp the trip until they got back to Europe.

“Route 66 is like Mount Everest,” he said. “You have to do it once in a lifetime.”

Every year, thousands of travelers cross America on Historic Route 66, a 2,500-mile stretch that was once the country’s most famous roadway. About a third of these road warriors are from overseas, and they're often searching for a glimpse of a lost era filled with motels, neon signs and hokey roadside attractions. This summer, I followed a dozen German and Swiss bikers on Harleys to to experience America through their eyes.

item.title: Getting Benefits of Retirement Home Care, at Your Own Home
item.description:
Not a single step interrupts the path, lined with thyme, to the front door of Joan Brasier’s ranch house in Asheville, N.C. With its remodeled primary bath and easy-to-clean surfaces, Ms. Brasier intends to stay in her home with her husband, Paul Wilczynski, for the foreseeable future.

It’s the unforeseeable, though, that has worried them. She and Mr. Wilczynski, both retired, want to travel. But they were concerned about spending money for fun today that they may need for care tomorrow, even though their careful calculations showed they could most likely afford it.

The couple found a solution in a little-known retirement model of care that is gaining momentum. “Continuing care at home,” provided through a continuing care retirement community, blends the expertise of those communities with support for members staying in their own homes. Members of these programs can move into the facility they contract with, if they need to, with the assurance of containing future costs.

About 75 percent of American adults in a 2024 AARP survey said they hoped to stay in their longtime homes, or “age in place,” as long as possible, with only 29 percent of older adults in the survey saying the traditional continuing care model was a likely choice. That model not only involves moving but requires a hefty entry fee and monthly fees to live on-site, where residents can transition to higher levels of care as their needs dictate. The at-home model has been operated by a few communities for decades, creating enough of a track record for the long-term-care industry to adopt it more widely.

This option is offered by only 37 of the country’s 1,911 continuing care retirement communities, or C.C.R.C.s, according to an industry group, LeadingAge, up from 26 a decade ago. More are exploring the concept, as evidenced by the escalating participation in the group’s conference on the topic.

Ms. Brasier, 74, and Mr. Wilczynski, 78, enrolled in Givens Choice, a three-year-old operation of Givens Communities in western North Carolina. The program provides regular health check-ins and coaching with a geriatric care specialist, known as the care manager, with the assurance of long-term care in a facility, at a fixed price.

“If we need a little bit of help, we get a little bit of help,” Ms. Brasier said. “If we need to go into care, we go into care.”

Depending on a person’s health and projected needs, Givens Choice’s plans start with a one-time fee that typically ranges from $33,000 to $77,000, for members entering at age 65 in good health, plus monthly care-management fees starting around $570. The program fees are for individuals, though couples receive a slight discount, said Erin Strain, executive director of the program.

Like all such programs, Givens Choice holds the entry fee to apply to future care expenses, while the monthly fee covers the check-ins and professional guidance — say, arranging in-home help like an aide or housekeeping — that enable members to stay in their homes as long as possible. A downside: The fee does not cover the cost of the in-home help. If at-home members need to move into the C.C.R.C. facility, they pay only the monthly fee (adjusted for inflation) that they had been paying all along.

For Ms. Brasier, the program swung into action a few months ago when she injured a shoulder in a fall while walking her dog. The couple’s Givens Choice care manager, already familiar with the household, stepped in to arrange at-home services that buoyed Ms. Brasier through the worst of her recovery. The monthly fee covered the manager’s work, and even some meal delivery. Medicare covered her health care.

Affordable late-in-life care is the holy grail for millions of American families. The latest data from Pew Research found that while most people hoped to age at home, they weren’t sure if they could. Of those who hoped to age in place with caregiver help, according to Pew research released in February, 37 percent said they thought they could pull it off.

Traditional continuing care retirement communities address many of these issues, but at a high price. Nationwide, the typical entry fee for on-site living ranges from $400,000 to $700,000, according to LeadingAge, although it can be lower or higher. It’s not uncommon for people to use proceeds from selling their home to pay that fee, yet the median home equity for homeowners 65 and older is $250,000, leaving a big gap. The cost is daunting for many families, especially if they hope to preserve their home equity for their heirs.

The at-home care model costs much less than the traditional option because members continues to pay any mortgage, insurance, taxes and maintenance on their properties. While members can gain access to some on-site community amenities, such as cultural programs and fitness facilities, they remain responsible for their own meals and daily costs of living. For on-site residents, monthly fees typically include meals, property maintenance, most utilities and other basic living expenses.

For admission, at-home members must pass a battery of physical and cognitive tests that are more stringent than for on-site residents. (Cognitive decline is the most common reason for being disqualified by Givens, Ms. Strain said.) Thus, at-home members usually join in their mid-70s, about eight years younger than the average on-site C.C.R.C. resident. An organization expects to collect monthly care fees for years before people become infirm, and also invests entry fees, according to executives at several C.C.R.C.s.

Timing your application for care at home is everything, said Paul Stavros, vice president of the Vibrant Life at Home division of Sun Health in Arizona. Begun in 2016, it has over 220 members in the western Phoenix area. He and other industry executives said that enrolling early and in good health increased the chances of being accepted and reduced the initial cost.

Each continuing care organization sets its own pricing structure for at-home programs, but across the country, the entry fees typically range from about $50,000 to hundreds of thousands per person, with members signing contracts outlining their fee structure and projected future costs.

All fees are tied to the prospective member’s age and health status and the type of contract that he or she buys. Some contracts are all inclusive, while others have co-pays for the cost of care, some up to 50 percent.

If a member later wants to cancel, any refund is dictated by the contract. At least three states — New York, North Carolina and New Hampshire — have specific regulations regarding at-home care plan cancellations, according to LeadingAge.

Fundamentally, the at-home programs act as a form of long-term-care insurance, integrated with monthly care and wellness management.

The numbers work for both the organizations and the individuals because it’s basic insurance-style math, said Brad Paulis, a partner with Continuing Care Actuaries. (Typically, C.C.R.C.s are regulated by state insurance departments, though they technically are not insurers.)

The at-home programs, Mr. Paulis said, pull money from a pool of healthy people and help keep members healthier longer, achieving individual longevity goals while minimizing risk for the organization.

Thirty percent of older Americans die before they need any late-in-life institutional care, Mr. Paulis said. “Another 40 percent use minimal care — under 90 days, before end of life. That’s why long-term-care policies have deductible periods,” he said, referring to the period that consumers must wait for payouts. The final 30 percent of Americans will have substantial long-term care bills, he said.

Despite the complexity of the C.C.R.C. options, the at-home model appears to fill a caregiving gap — if families can learn about it in time for elder relatives to qualify. Here is what potential members need to do before applying.

Scout and compare at-home programs, as organizations are figuring out how to market them and information about pilots may be difficult to find.

Cut through confusing language: Many C.C.R.C.s call people on their regular waiting lists “at home” residents, said Margaret Johnson, a senior director with Fitch Ratings, which assesses the financial status of C.C.R.C.s. Ask for clarity.

Calculate the cost of staying at home, like making modifications to your house and choosing and managing at-home services. “Only 14 percent of middle-income older adults can afford four or more hours a day of in-home health care,” said Lisa McCracken, head of research and analytics for the National Investment Center for Seniors Housing and Care. “That tells us that for them, aging in place is not always a great plan, either.”

Couples must assess how they’ll manage and pay for care if their needs and health diverge. One spouse may have a progressive disease while the other’s health is more stable. Often, programs offer support and care coordination to both spouses, even if the contract covers only the healthier spouse, said Dee Pekruhn, senior director of life plan communities and continuing care at home with LeadingAge.

Consider your friendships and other social connections, which you could cultivate by living in a facility rather than at home. At-home care may exacerbate isolation, which can put older people’s health at greater risk.

Lesley Morter said she wished she had known about such programs several years ago, when her mother, now 88, was still living in her own home. As Ms. Morter was exploring options, the family’s plans crumbled.

Now, Ms. Morter, 60, is trying to patch together a strategy to ensure that her mother’s care plan at least keeps pace with her income — a seemingly impossible task.

With her mother’s house sold and her capabilities erratic, Ms. Morter and her family are finding that the puzzle pieces don’t fit. “We’re scrambling,” she said.

item.title: Oil Prices Rise Slightly After U.S. and Iran Trade Strikes
item.description:
Oil prices rose slightly on Sunday after the United States and Iran traded attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz in recent days, leaving a vital oil export route stuck in what analysts described as a lethal stalemate.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, was up about 1 percent to nearly $97 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, was also about 1 percent higher, at a little over $92 a barrel.

OPEC Plus, the cartel of influential oil-producing nations that helps control oil prices by coordinating supply decisions, opted on Sunday to keep production flat for October. It was the first time since April that the organization decided against increasing production. The increases, though, have been largely symbolic because the Iran war has disrupted exports and the worldwide oil trade.

The national average price for a gallon of gas was nearly $4.15 through Sunday, according to the AAA motor club. The Labor Day weekend is traditionally a road-trip heavy period.

AAA said the price was the highest average it had ever recorded for this time of year. The previous record of $3.82 a gallon for Labor Day weekend was set in September 2012. But, adjusting for inflation, that price surpassed this weekend’s. (The 2012 price would today translate to an average price of $5.51, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’s inflation calculator.)

Rising fuel prices also affected holiday weekend air travel: AAA said tickets on flights to 10 of the most popular domestic destinations — including Orlando, Fla., New York and Las Vegas — were up nearly 20 percent compared with last year.

Oil and gas prices have risen sharply since the Iran war began in at the end of February, choking off shipments through the strait. Brent crude has risen more than 33 percent since the war’s start, and West Texas Intermediate crude has jumped a little over 37 percent. The national average price of regular gas has increased nearly 40 percent from its prewar average of $2.98 per gallon.

The U.S. military’s protection efforts have helped get millions of barrels of oil out of the Persian Gulf each day, but attacks from Iran have made the trip extremely risky. Two crew members on a Saudi vessel were killed last week when their ship was struck near Oman’s coast.

The war between Russia and Ukraine has added pressure through disabling strikes on Russian oil refineries, leaving the world with less capacity to turn oil into gasoline and diesel.

item.title: A Tidier Rivian (in Size and Price) Is Ready for the Suburbs
item.description:
Rivian, after four years selling its R1S, a hulking three-row electric S.U.V. that easily reaches six-figure prices, is making the leap into the mainstream.

Nipping at Tesla’s heels, Rivian recently introduced a highly anticipated smaller (and more affordable) S.U.V. aimed at the upscale masses.

It’s called the R2, but a more appropriate name would have been the R2.0.

That’s because this new sport utility (which is shorter by 15 inches, and 2,000 pounds lighter) incorporates many of the things R1S owners said they missed. (Rivian also makes a truck, the R1T.) The R2 still features advanced software, off-road capabilities, a whisper-quiet cabin, decent range and probably the most comfortable seats of any vehicle I’ve ever driven.

Not only are the price and dimensions of this new version closer to what most American buyers want, but the R2 addresses many of the R1S’s shortfalls.

Once even less-expensive variants become available next year, the two-row R2 looks to become an American hit for those looking for a high-tech electric S.U.V. that’s capable both on the road and off.

Kevin Duffin, a former Tesla owner, was looking forward to being one of the first to buy an R2. After driving a Model 3 for four years, he was ready for an E.V. with more creature comforts.

The sparse Tesla interior turned Mr. Duffin off. “It was like a Scandinavian living room,” he said. A travel industry executive in Los Angeles, Mr. Duffin put himself on the waiting list for an R2. But when he saw the R1S at a pop-up event, he decided he couldn’t wait and bought one of those instead. Now he has had second thoughts.

“If I had to do it again, I’d lean toward the R2,” he said. “I don’t need three rows of seats. And the R2 is better value for money.”

The R2 adds many features expected in a full-size S.U.V. but are missing in the R1S. Where the larger R1S has no glove box, the R2 has two. Unlike the R1S’s fixed rear glass, the R2’s retracts, allowing large loads to be carried with the rear hatch closed. Put a mobile phone down on the R1S’s charging pad and it’ll slip and slide and disconnect as you drive; the R2 adds a magnet for grip.

Storage abounds, with multiple nooks and crannies to hold stuff; there’s even a pullout shelf for a long box of tissues. Stanley fans don’t fret; your mega thermoses will fit in a molded corner of both front doors.

Unlike the R1S, the R2 is small enough for Rivian to have made plans to sell it in Europe, with manufacturing done in a plant outside Atlanta that will open in 2028.

The top-of-the-line Launch Edition is available now and priced close to $58,000, and Rivian expects to sell lower-featured versions starting at $45,000 next year. Contrast that with the R1S, which starts at around $80,000 and tops out at $122,000, before taxes.

Its federal mileage on a full charge ranges from 275 to 345, depending on whether it’s a long-range trim and an all-wheel or rear-wheel drive model.

A number of factors helped bring down costs, Rivian’s founder, R.J. Scaringe, said in a recent interview. The company, now more fully established, has improved supplier relationships and is able to get lower component prices.

“With the R1, I would go and meet with suppliers and they would be like, ‘I don’t want to work with you. Who are you?’ ” Mr. Scaringe said. Now things are different. “With the same supplier who I had to fly to meet, we now have in some cases the C.E.O.s flying to meet us.”

By consolidating and eliminating items, Rivian has cut the number of parts and the assembly cost to half those for the R1S, Mr. Scaringe said.

Yet this is no bare-bones vehicle. Unlike the Tesla, the R2 has a driver-facing screen as well as a center display, meaning the driver does not need to look away from the road to check speed or direction.

Seat heating, cooling and a Tesla-like “dog mode” keeps the cabin comfortable for both pets and people. Regenerative braking and drive modes can be customized for each driver.

Acceleration is quick, stability around corners solid. And the Rivian is the first vehicle in the U.S. to offer Matrix adaptive headlights, which can control individual sections of the beam and reduce glare for other drivers. (Some Teslas have them and Audi now also offers adaptive headlights on its upcoming Q9 S.U.V.)

Most of the vehicle functions are software-based. For the R2, Rivian has added two physical haptic wheels to either side of the steering wheel that control multiple functions such as changing the steering wheel position, adjusting the side mirrors, audio volume and more.

Unfortunately the wheels don’t always respond correctly; a push may do nothing, or register as a scroll, displaying information you didn’t want. Some functions that are elementary with physical controls become more complex when almost everything is on a screen.

While the cabin doesn’t want for storage space, it does for overhead grab handles, often found in the area above each seat; this could make it difficult for those with movement issues to get in and out. (It was partly a cost consideration, said Rivian’s head of design, Jeff Hammoud.)

With vehicles that use traditional knobs and buttons, turning on air recirculation is easy: just push a button. In the Rivian, one has to first push the temperature control on the center screen and then the air recirculation icon, taking your eyes off the road for a longer period.

Similarly, to adjust the exterior mirrors you touch your driver profile, then the left or right mirror adjustment icon, then actually adjust them by turning one of the two physical haptic knobs in the steering wheel.

As with the Tesla, neither Apple CarPlay nor Android Auto are offered. Instead, owners use a few built-in apps to navigate and listen to music, podcasts and books. Those include Apple Music, Audible, TuneIn and Spotify. Mr. Scaringe said others such as WhatsApp and Zoom would also be available eventually.

Also, you’ll need to pay for what you get free with CarPlay and Android Auto. Use of the built-in apps costs $150 a year for the Connect+ subscription, which also includes a Wi-Fi hot spot, voice assistant, Google satellite imagery, remote camera livestreaming and video app streaming. Without it, drivers must send the audio signal from a smartphone into the vehicle’s sound system via Bluetooth.

Software glitches are evident. On my test vehicle, screen icons did not always respond when pressed, and the rear lid didn’t always open when the button was touched. Strangely, to turn on the rear vents, one counterintuitively touches an icon in the front air control panel, not the panel for the rear.

Looking to learn how to open the rear hatch? You won’t find out by reading the owner’s manual. That’s because the hatch is called a “liftgate” in Rivian parlance. There’s no cross-reference to alternative common words.

The good news: All of these small issues are fixable with software updates. Rivian will be adding voice control (not noted in the manual) and with its Autonomy+ package, the ability to have the vehicle not just drive and change lanes on its own, but also to automatically traverse a freeway route, point to point. The Autonomy+ package costs $50 a month or $2,500 outright. (It’s included in the $58,000 Launch edition.)

Glitches and limitations aside, the R2 is an impressive vehicle in fit and finish, quality of materials, drive capabilities and comfort. As a software-defined vehicle, constant upgrades are possible as the company refines the experience and responds to consumer input. And it hits a price point aimed at the masses.

item.title: Social Media in China Is Getting Really Dark
item.description:
One of the hottest videos on the popular Chinese site Bilibili in the past two weeks is a quasi-serious guide on how to survive as a homeless person.

Sleep near garbage bins where “supplies” are replenished, use cardboard to insulate yourself from the damp and avoid surveillance cameras, the video suggested. It was viewed more than six million times and was briefly ranked the site’s No. 2 video.

Viewers jokingly called it “Youth Study,” the name of the Communist Youth League’s political education program, and “a required course for young people in 2026.”

The Chinese Communist Party has spent years trying to make “positive energy” the dominant mood of the country’s internet. Online platforms, it dictates, should amplify narratives of economic achievement, gratitude toward the party and confidence in China’s future.

Discontent has occasionally erupted after disasters, scandals or particularly brutal government actions. But something feels different lately. The pessimism is persistent. It has become part of the everyday social media feed, and can sometimes turn subversive.

China’s economic growth is slowing. A prolonged property crash has eroded the value of many families’ biggest asset while jobs have become harder to find and less secure. As the malaise deepens, more social media users are abandoning a cheery, compliant public performance and creating counternarratives that censorship can sometimes erase but not easily rebut.

Across RedNote, Douyin, Weibo and other popular platforms, you can scroll endless posts about meager wages, scarce jobs, falling property values and fear about the future. Some turn their hardships into dark humor. Others hijack official posts and hashtags and turn propaganda into spectacles of mockery.

China’s censorship apparatus still controls the internet. But prolonged economic distress is making it harder for the party to maintain its preferred account of how the country is doing.

China’s official youth unemployment rate reached 17.9 percent in July. More than 200 million people, over a quarter of the country’s working population, now work in what the government calls “flexible employment” — essentially a vast gig economy.

A hashtag on RedNote, also known as Xiaohongshu, urging people to keep a tight grip on their money has been viewed nearly 120 million times.

Young Chinese struggle to find jobs and are retreating from marriage and parenthood. Middle-age people who have followed the prescribed routes to security now feel that their major life decisions may have become liabilities.

“In this environment, you’ve won if you didn’t buy apartments, didn’t buy cars, didn’t invest or didn’t get married early,” read one post on RedNote. People born in the 1980s who strove the hardest, it said, are likely the biggest losers. The post was liked nearly 2,000 times.

The criticism sometimes extends to forbidden territory — the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Communist Party rule.

In November, the comment section on a Douyin post explaining the idiom “yichou wannian,” — literally, “to leave a stench for 10,000 years,” or to be remembered in infamy forever — blew up. Users made veiled references to Mr. Xi, who is often referred to simply as “he” in Chinese conversations. “He’s in a league of his own,” one comment said.

Li Ying, known for his online alias, “Teacher Li,” runs a popular account on X that serves as an uncensored information clearinghouse about China. He and his team monitor the Chinese social media sphere closely. They’ve seen an “exponential” increase in pessimistic and even subversive posts and comments this year, he said.

“Back in 2022, if we saw one online comment mocking Xi Jinping, we considered it worth sharing because few people dared say things like that,” Mr. Li said. “Today, you see so much of it that it barely even registers anymore.”

As the economy declined, people started asking questions that they didn’t need to think of before, Mr. Li said. Many users may not have realized that their personal complaints could be considered political. For example, he said, some government workers on RedNote compared how many months they had gone without getting paid.

To the social media users, their individual posts might feel like a personal reflection or complaint. But collectively they offer an account of China at odds with the official narrative of progress and prosperity.

Other users are deliberately using social media as a tool of dissent, and they subvert official propaganda to that purpose. A Douyin video proclaiming the Communist Party to be the world’s greatest party drew 41,000 roughly identical comments with rows of crying-face emojis punctuated by slashes and backslashes.

The tactic becomes especially potent when users converge on government and state media accounts. Last month, a state-affiliated media post claimed that China had invented human flight during the Ming dynasty, centuries before the West. The post triggered many sarcastic comments. “I get withdrawal symptoms if I go a day without hearing that China has won,” one said. “When will we invent two-day weekends?” said another.

Christian Göbel, a professor of contemporary Chinese politics at the University of Vienna, calls this tactic “subversive amplification.” Rather than build an audience of their own, users piggyback on the reach of official posts while undermining their intended messages.

China’s internet censorship has grown increasingly ruthless over the past decade. That makes the sheer volume of the pessimistic posts and sarcastic comments all the more striking. At the same time, it’s difficult to know why some posts survive long enough to go viral while others quickly disappear.

One possible explanation is that policing too aggressively could hurt traffic and advertising revenue. Another potential explanation is that recommendation algorithms allow scattered grievances to find one another.

When I opened my RedNote in recent weeks, I was surprised to find that the first 30 or so posts were nearly all about economic despair, many with hundreds or thousands of likes. The suggested searches could be even gloomier. “Is there a future for employment in China?” read one.

The government has tried to tamp down on negative energy. In 2023, the Ministry of State Security portrayed efforts to “bad-mouth China’s economy” as a security and political issue. Last year, the internet regulator ordered platforms to suppress claims that hard work or education was useless, as well as memes and jokes that excessively spread pessimism.

In April, the Ministry of State Security posted an article accusing an unnamed foreign organization of funding “lying flat” influencers to “erode the minds of Chinese youth.” “Lying flat” is a growing trend among young Chinese people who believe that striving is futile in the face of a bleak economic future.

The accusation prompted another counternarrative. Under a related hashtag on Weibo, users connected “lying flat” to scarce jobs, low wages and punishing work schedules. Some questioned whether the government was desperate. “When the mule stops working, the landlord stops making money,” one commenter wrote.

The ministry closed the article’s comment section.

“I don’t know if this can really be controlled,” Mr. Göbel said. “Any narrative that would try to make this go away would be an insult to the people who are suffering.”
